abstract: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to provide continuous personalized assistance by retaining user information across interactions. Existing systems support this process through fact extraction, organization, updating, and retrieval, but largely maintain memories as independent facts. This fact-centric paradigm may overlook how new facts update, constrain, or conflict with earlier ones, while leaving their applicability, role, and priority for the current request implicit. In this paper, we introduce EvoMemState, a state-centric framework that augments persistent facts with two complementary states: Relational States that capture how facts remain valid and relate to one another as memory evolves, and a Reasoning State that determines how these facts should be applied to the current request. Specifically, EvoMemState consists of three key components: (i) Ontology-Guided Memory State Induction extracts Persistent Facts and constructs Relational States that maintain their validity, scope, and evolving relations. (ii) RL-Based State Evolution internalizes memory-use experience into a policy through reinforcement learning to generate a request-specific Reasoning State. (iii) State-Aware Reasoning then combines the relevant facts with their Relational States and the generated Reasoning State to guide the personal agent. Extensive experiments on long-term dialogue and memory-use benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over existing memory systems in retrieval completeness and memory-grounded response accuracy. Our code and implementation details are available at https://github.com/XMUDeepLIT/EvoMemState.git.

sections.body: Personal agents need memory that stays consistent across sessions. Existing systems extract, organize, update, and retrieve facts, but treat them as independent records, which can leave updates and conflicts unresolved. The authors propose EvoMemState, which keeps Persistent Facts and adds two states: Relational States for validity, scope, and relations, and a Reasoning State for how facts apply to the current request. Two challenges are named: building coherent states as information arrives, and learning memory-use strategies from experience. The contributions are the problem analysis, the framework, and evaluation on long-term dialogue and memory-use benchmarks.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Fact-centric memory systems miss how facts update and conflict, motivating a state-centric framework with three components.

sections.body: Two preliminary studies use the Valid Memory Selection subset of MemSyco-Bench, where correct answers depend on memories linked by updates, conflicts, or constraints. The first asks whether fact-centric systems retrieve related memories together. Figure 2 reports that MemoryBank, LightMem, and Supermemory miss relevant information in 58.9%, 61.8%, and 58.0% of cases, and that for four of five systems accuracy is 5.9–33.3% higher when all required memories are retrieved. The second gives agents all relevant memories and compares direct answering with a fixed self-reflection step. Self-reflection lowers average accuracy from 50.5% to 48.9%, so full access does not ensure appropriate use. The authors conclude that memory relations and learned memory-use strategies are needed.
sections.heading: Preliminary Studies
sections.headline: Preliminary studies find related memories are often not retrieved together, and full retrieval does not ensure correct use.

sections.body: The method has three parts. Ontology-Guided Memory State Induction extracts Persistent Facts from each conversation, inserts them in temporal order into an ontology with `PARENT_OF`, `CONTAINS`, `SUPERSEDES`, and `CONFLICTS_WITH` edges, and derives a Relational State for each fact without overwriting it. RL-Based State Evolution trains a Memory State Evolution Policy with GRPO. Each candidate Reasoning State is scored by how much it improves a frozen personal agent's answer over a baseline that receives the same evidence. At inference, `K` seed facts are retrieved and expanded through memory relations, and the policy generates a Reasoning State that the agent uses together with the facts.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Method builds an ontology of facts, trains a policy to generate Reasoning States, and reasons over both states.

sections.body: Experiments compare EvoMemState with nine baselines on MemSyco-Bench, MemTrapBench, LoCoMo, and LoCoMo-Refined. With Qwen3-8B and GPT-4o-mini, EvoMemState reaches 57.6% and 58.9% accuracy on MemSyco-Bench, outperforming the strongest baselines by 12.2% and 5.9%. In ablations with Qwen3-8B, removing the Relational State lowers the MemSyco-Bench average from 57.6 to 48.7, and removing RL-Based State Evolution lowers the MemTrap average from 79.1 to 62.7. Figure 5 reports complete retrieval and accuracy on complete-evidence cases. Pairing the learned policy with other memory systems improves all six baselines, with gains from 0.2% to 4.9%.
sections.heading: Experiment
sections.headline: Experiments show gains over nine baselines on memory-use and dialogue benchmarks, with each component contributing in ablations.

sections.body: Related work covers two areas. The first is personal agents and user modeling. LaMP retrieves profile items for personalized generation, HELLO and related methods maintain user representations over time, and PGMem links persona information to events that support or revise it. The second is long-term memory systems. MemGPT manages information across storage tiers, MemoryBank maintains personal records, LightMem uses compression and selective retrieval, and Mem0 extracts and updates facts. A-MEM, Supermemory, and SimpleMem further organize memories through links, temporal structure, and update mechanisms.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work covers personal user modeling and long-term memory systems that maintain and organize user information.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes EvoMemState as a state-centric long-term memory framework for personal agents. It constructs Relational States from multi-source memories and learns from continual memory use to generate Reasoning States. The section reports consistent improvements across memory-use and dialogue-recall benchmarks, particularly under preference updates and conflicting evidence. It concludes that reliable personal memory requires both coherent state construction and use-driven state evolution.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The conclusion states that reliable personal memory needs both coherent state construction and use-driven state evolution.

sections.body: This limitation section states that the study focuses on text-based interaction histories. Real-world personal memory systems must also handle multimodal information, including documents, images, and other user artifacts. The authors identify representing, connecting, and applying information across modalities as an important direction for future work.
sections.heading: Limitation
sections.headline: The method handles only text histories, leaving multimodal personal information such as documents and images for future work.

sections.body: The appendix begins with frequently asked questions that explain the personal memory ontology, the Reasoning State, and the choice of a separate policy over self-reflection. Appendix B gives the full formulation of Persistent Facts, Relational States, and Reasoning States, the ontology construction and validation rules, and the GRPO training setup. Appendix C covers a case study and efficiency analysis. Appendix D describes datasets, baselines, metrics, and implementation settings, Appendix E lists prompts, and Appendix F gives extended related work. Further figures show ontology operations, case analyses, rule examples, and baseline configurations.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists frequently asked questions, method details, prompts, extended related work, and figures for case studies and efficiency.
